source.note: Generated by `--plan brief.md` with z-ai/glm-5.3-flash (second attempt; the first wrote done_threshold 1, out of bounds), then approved with these edits, applied by plans/approve_ja.py. (1) Every rubric came back best-first; the program reads level 0 as the worst, so each question's rubric and the fit rubric were reversed. The fit rubric was also reordered so that 'cannot be assessed' sits above 'irreconcilable conflict'. (2) per_dimension 1 -> 2, min_q 5 -> 8, max_q 8 -> 12, reserve_early 1 (unchanged): as written, coverage was met by the fourth answer and the budget ran to eight, so the judge chose almost nothing and `done` could not vary. Now 4 dimensions owe 8 answers, the budget is 12, and the pool is 16. (3) done_threshold 0.95 -> 0.5: the model's two attempts wrote 1 and then the bound's maximum, neither a considered number; 0.5 is the same provisional value the earlier 50-interview plan ran under. (4) Six questions added by the approver, written in the same style, so the pool exceeds the budget and some questions go unasked: two per technical dimension. A second generated draft failed validation twice and was not used. (5) ui text -> textarea, with text also allowed: these questions want prose. (6) One typo fixed in rust_readiness (聞かせます -> 聞かせてください). (7) done.true: 'at least once' -> 'at least twice', to match per_dimension. Nothing else was changed; dimension names and weights are the model's. The English plan is a translation of the approved Japanese plan made at approval time; ids, order, policy and rubric levels are identical.

answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: Our wallet-service wraps the payout write in one transaction; a senior engineer, Priya, set that boundary before I joined. I added a new column and a read method inside it last year, under her review. I haven't had to move a boundary myself. When I asked why it's structured that way, she said it keeps balance updates atomic with the payout row, and I've taken that as correct rather than testing it myself.
answers.says: Has no experience making transaction boundary design decisions themselves. The answer stops at ‘the team decided’ or ‘a senior engineer designed it,’ and even when asked what part they were responsible for or what they considered, they cannot explain concretely. They claim Java experience, but the answer shows the design decisions were left to others.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: Our SRE team owns GC tuning and Kubernetes config for wallet-service; I've sat in on two incident calls where they adjusted heap size, but I didn't do the diagnosis myself. Once I bumped a connection pool from 10 to 20 on Priya's instruction after a dashboard she was watching showed wait times climbing. I couldn't tell you the exact numbers behind that call, just that it worked.
answers.says: Explains that JVM and Kubernetes operations were handled by other team members or SRE, so they only wrote code and were never directly involved in operational problems. Even when asked about their involvement in triage or measurement, they cannot describe concretely what logs they looked at or what action they took.

answers.text: I'd like to check something from your earlier answers where you used the phrase 'as a team.' Within that, which parts did you personally decide and do yourself? Please answer the same question again, using a different piece of experience.
answers.answer: Fair question. In the payout write-path I described, the part that was really mine was adding the new balance column and its read method; Priya designed the transaction boundary and the retry/dedupe table. In a different case, updating our on-call runbook, I wrote the whole document myself but the escalation policy inside it came from my lead.
answers.says: Names a concrete example from their earlier answers, and clearly separates the points they decided alone (a design choice, incident triage, deciding a migration boundary, etc.) from the points left to the team. Can explain, in their own words, the grounds for the decision and the part they did hands-on, and can do the same for a different piece of experience. Comes with numbers and time frames, so 'as a team' is described as an actual division of labor rather than a convenient phrase.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: I haven't built idempotency handling myself. Our payout retries go through a Kafka consumer with a dedupe table that a senior engineer designed before I joined; I've read the code but never had to design or fix that mechanism, and I've never had a duplicate-payout incident land on my desk to debug.
answers.says: Has no real example of duplication or a mismatch they personally handled; the answer stops at ‘the team handled it,’ and even when asked about their own role, they cannot explain concretely. Or, they cannot describe any experience handling a consistency mismatch at all.

answers.text: Tell me about a concrete incident where the numbers didn't match in settlement or reconciliation. What was off, by how much, how did you notice, what was the cause, and how did you correct it? Please also cover how you handled data after it was finalized.
answers.answer: I haven't chased down a reconciliation mismatch myself. I know we run a nightly job that compares wallet balances to the payment processor's records, and I've seen its output in Slack, but investigating a mismatch has always gone to a senior engineer, not to me.
answers.says: Cannot describe any experience of chasing down a numeric mismatch at all. Even the explanation of the reconciliation concept is vague, or the answer drifts into unrelated career history.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I told my lead the same day I shipped a null-check bug that caused a small spike in failed payout requests, maybe 40 of them, rather than waiting to see if anyone noticed. I've done on-call for about eight months, one week in six, mostly routing pages to a senior since I can't fix most issues alone yet.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: I haven't personally restored broken production data. There was a missing-journal-entry issue in wallet-service before I joined that a senior fixed with a backfill script; I only know about it from the incident doc, not from doing the work.
answers.says: Explains that restoring consistency was handled by a DBA or a different team, so they weren't involved. Even when asked about scoping or verification, they cannot describe concretely what they looked at or what they did.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: There was a payout duplication incident about a year ago, before I'd been on wallet-service long enough to be on the response. I heard about it in the postmortem doc but wasn't part of triage or the fix. The closest I've come to incident response myself is restarting a stuck consumer once, at a senior's direction.
answers.says: Has no experience with an incident in a system they themselves operated; the answer stays at what they heard or saw about an incident someone else handled. Cannot describe their own role concretely even when asked.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I haven't written Rust in production, just Rustlings exercises this year, maybe 15 hours total. My plan is to finish those, then build a small CLI that parses our payout CSV exports, over the next two months, before touching anything with async. I think ownership will take longest to click. On boundaries, I'd lean on whoever's done a migration before rather than guess.
answers.says: Can describe Rust terminology accurately (ownership, lifetimes, tokio, etc.), but gives no real example of code they wrote or ran themselves. On migration too, the answer stays at generalities like ‘Rust should be adopted because it's safe and fast,’ without describing how to decide a boundary or what to measure as their own judgment. The explanation of the difference from Java reads like a summary of an introductory book, and the learning plan is no more than ‘I'll study it,’ with no realism visible.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: Honestly I don't have a real answer here yet. If asked to move part of a ledger write path, I'd want to sit with a senior engineer first and watch what they measure, since I've never made that call myself. My guess is you'd watch latency and error counts, but I'd rather admit I'm guessing than make it sound like experience I have.
answers.says: Has no experience making boundary-design or migration decisions themselves, and even when pressed, gives nothing beyond reciting general principles. Cannot construct a concrete plan of their own for where to start.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I pushed back once on adding a new wallet-balance cache, saying it could go stale, but I didn't have data, just a hunch, and the team went with it anyway. I didn't build a competing version afterward; I helped implement the agreed cache and watched to see if my worry showed up, which it didn't.
answers.says: Can describe voicing a disagreement, but the argument was based on feeling or preference rather than evidence, and they cannot describe what they did after the decision. The answer stops at ‘in the end, the team's approach won out,’ with nothing on how they accepted the decision and acted on it.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: I haven't been in a situation urgent enough to be tempted to skip review. Our deploy pipeline requires one approval regardless, and I've always waited for it, even when a fix felt obvious. I think skipping would need real, ongoing harm and someone else's sign-off recorded somewhere, not just my own sense that I'm right.
answers.says: On skipping the procedure in an emergency, says in general terms that ‘the principle should be upheld,’ but has no real example of being forced to make that call themselves, and the answer stays theoretical. Or the answer stays at ‘it depends on the situation,’ without giving concrete criteria for where they personally would draw the line. Technically correct understanding, but with no experience behind it.

fit.says: The candidate is broadly aligned with most of the working principles, but shows a conditional attitude in some areas — for example, saying something to the effect of ‘in an emergency, you should fix it first even if it means skipping the procedure,’ without committing to announcing and recording that skip, or not speaking positively about on-call or support work. They could work here, but some coaching would be needed to bring them fully in line with the principles.
